description:
Hi! I'm Gul Nawaz, a GIS Specialist and Remote Sensing/GIS Master's student based in Pakistan. My expertise lies in Google Earth Engine, spatial machine learning, and full-stack WebGIS development (Python, PostgreSQL/PostGIS, and JS mapping libraries like Leaflet/Mapbox).

Why You Should Join "Team Pixel Alpha": We are tackling a high-level Earth observation challenge: building a robust data harmonization pipeline for MODIS and VIIRS satellite data.
summary:
Satellites have tracked fires for more than 20 years, but the record is split. MODIS has flown since 2000, and VIIRS joined in 2012 with sharper pixels that catch many more small fires. Simply adding them together makes fire counts jump every time a new satellite launches. Over Pakistan, the raw count rose almost seven times from 2011 to 2012 even though real burning barely changed.

We built Burning Calendar to fix this. Using NASA FIRMS hotspots, we express everything in one unit, S-NPP VIIRS detections. A machine learning model trained on the years both sensors overlap rebuilds 2000 to 2011, and NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 fill any gaps. When we predicted years the model had never seen, monthly totals matched with correlations of 0.97 to 0.995.

A web app puts this consistent record on a map. Anyone can draw an area and see when it burns, which years were worst and whether this month is unusual, then download the data. It already covers Pakistan, Northwest India and Argentina. This gives fire managers and researchers a fire history they can actually trust as MODIS nears retirement.

Links
Live app: https://neon-chebakia-dba7e4.netlify.app
Code (GitHub): https://github.com/Gull01/Burning-Calendar-Harmonization
Slides: https://nustedupk0-my.sharepoint.com/:p:/g/personal/gnawaz_ms24igis_student_nust_edu_pk/IQA1r17Gk_JqQ7xqvIYzlc3nAUAxuZrYYe2dqGh6V5V3_rA?e=Tdt2EN

How it works
The fire record is split between two sensors. MODIS has flown since 2000 with 1 km pixels. VIIRS joined in 2012 with 375 m pixels and sees many small fires MODIS misses. Every new satellite (S-NPP in 2012, NOAA-20 in 2018, NOAA-21 in 2023) makes raw counts jump. Over Pakistan, adding all satellites together made the count rise 6.7 times between 2011 and 2012, while Aqua MODIS on its own barely moved.

We fixed one reference, S-NPP VIIRS, and express everything in that unit. For the years both sensors flew, a gradient boosting model learns how what MODIS saw in each grid cell and month relates to what S-NPP saw. It uses hotspot counts, unique pixels, day and night detections, fire radiative power and activity in the surrounding area. It works on log counts and is calibrated by calendar month. The model then rebuilds VIIRS-equivalent counts for 2000 to 2011. When S-NPP has a data gap, NOAA-20 or NOAA-21 fills it, scaled to S-NPP. Before any of this, we keep only vegetation fires, drop low-confidence detections and remove persistent industrial heat sources such as brick kilns and gas flares.

We tested it the way it is used. Trained only on 2017 onward, the model predicted 2013 to 2016, years it never saw. Monthly totals matched with a correlation of 0.972 for Pakistan, 0.988 for Northwest India and 0.995 for Argentina, with an overall bias of 2.5 to 5.1 percent. The pipeline also runs a simple ratio method on the same test and keeps whichever does better, so a weak model cannot slip through.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Fire and disaster managers can see at a glance whether this month is unusual for their area, and plan monitoring around the real burning seasons.
  • Researchers and environment agencies get a long, consistent record for trend analysis that keeps going as MODIS retires.
  • Air quality teams can link smoke episodes to the burning season behind them, for example rice residue burning in October and November in Pakistan.
  • The method is open, so any country can rebuild its own record from FIRMS files.

The tool already finds real stories. October crop burning in Pakistan is now more than four times its 2002 to 2011 level. The busiest years it finds in Argentina, 2020, 2003 and 2008, match the major Paraná Delta fire seasons. In Northwest India, detected burning has dropped sharply since 2021. Studies report that some farmers there now burn after the afternoon satellite passes, so the app warns users not to over-read that decline.

Tools and technologies

  • Data: NASA FIRMS active fire data, MODIS Collection 6.1 (Terra, Aqua) and VIIRS 375 m (S-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21), archive and near real-time.
  • Pipeline: Python with pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn (gradient boosting), Matplotlib and PyArrow.
  • Web app: HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Leaflet, Leaflet.draw and D3. There is no server: data is packed into compact binary files and the site is hosted on Netlify.
  • Map tiles: Esri and OpenStreetMap.
  • Hardware: our own laptops; no special hardware needed.

What makes it creative

  • Instead of pooling all satellites, we chose one fixed reference sensor, so the record no longer depends on how many satellites are flying.
  • We validated it backwards, in the same direction we rebuild the early years, not just with standard cross validation.
  • The app judges the current month fairly even halfway through, by comparing it with what usually happens by the same day.
  • Each cell is compared with its own usual, so a quiet desert cell and a busy farming cell can be read on the same map.

Factors we considered

  • Honesty about uncertainty: years before 2012 are marked as rebuilt, and the app explains the method and its limits in a “How it works” panel.
  • Real zeros versus missing data: the pipeline tells “no fire seen” apart from “no satellite data”, and detects outages automatically.
  • Accessibility: colour scales readable with colour vision deficiency, clear labels, and a layout that works on phones.
  • Speed and cost: the whole app runs as a static site with no server, so it is free to host and fast to load.
  • Reuse: the pipeline works for any region with FIRMS data, and the code is open under the MIT licence.
